title: The Miracle Equation
research_note: Full text not read (borrow-only / paywalled). Secondary summaries only. facts.claim: The book is The Miracle Equation by Hal Elrod, published by Harmony; ebook and audiobook listed April 2019. Subtitle: The Two Decisions That Move Your Biggest Goals from Possible, to Probable, to Inevitable.
The equation is Unwavering Faith + Extraordinary Effort = Miracles; the two decisions are unwavering faith and extraordinary effort.

Unwavering faith is described as a vow to yourself to stick to one goal no matter what is going on externally or how you feel internally, with no excuses; also as complete belief in the goal and in your ability to achieve it. Setbacks will happen and faith is what gets you back up.

Extraordinary effort is described as consistency: focused, persistent action built from small daily steps; 'the key to success is not one remarkable action, but a series of small actions that you take every day.'

Goal advice: choose one overarching mission instead of many goals, like an Olympic athlete focusing on one sport; break it into monthly targets for urgency; reshape the environment to remove obstacles (example: gym clothes kept in the car); micro-steps; block time on the calendar.
Chapter titles include 'Your Mission', 'Your First Decision: Unwavering Faith', 'Your Second Decision: Extraordinary Effort', 'Maintaining Miracles', plus a 30-Day Challenge.
Two types of miracles: passive (unexplainable, beyond control) and active/created (made through belief, determination and work). People who pursue active miracles are called Miracle Mavens.
Passive miracle example: Donnie Register, working in an antique store, was about to be shot; he raised his hands to his face and the bullet bounced off his gold wedding ring.

The Five-Minute Rule for emotional pain: when something bad happens, give yourself a fixed window of five minutes (set a timer) to feel it however you need (cry, complain, scream); when time is up say 'can't change it' out loud and move on.

Elrod's framing: suffering is the direct result of resisting our reality; emotional pain rarely has to do with what happens to us but with how we respond. Peace means accepting what you cannot change, not being happy about it.
Quote attributed to the book: 'The real purpose of every goal you set is to become the type of person who can consistently set and achieve significant goals.'
